title: Enlil
wiki_lead:
Enlil (Sumerian: 𒀭𒂗𒆤 dEN-LÍL), later known as Elil and Ellil, is an ancient Mesopotamian god associated with wind, air, earth, and storms. He is first attested as the chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, but he was later worshipped by the Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, and Hurrians. Enlil's primary center of worship was the Ekur temple in the city of Nippur, which was believed to have been built by Enlil himself and was regarded as the "mooring-rope" of heaven and earth. He is also sometimes referred to in Sumerian texts as Nunamnir. According to one Sumerian hymn, Enlil himself was so holy that not even the other gods could look upon him. Enlil rose to prominence during the twenty-fourth century BC with the rise of Nippur. His cult fell into decline after Nippur was sacked by the Elamites in 1230 BC and he was eventually supplanted as the chief god of the Mesopotamian pantheon by the Babylonian national god Marduk.
Enlil plays a vital role in the ancient near eastern cosmology; he separates An (heaven) from Ki (earth), thus making the world habitable for humans. In the Sumerian flood myth Eridu Genesis, Enlil rewards Ziusudra with immortality for having survived the flood and, in the Babylonian flood myth, Enlil is the cause of the flood himself, having sent the flood to exterminate the human race, who made too much noise and prevented him from sleeping; the cuneiform tablets of Atra-Hasis report on this connections in a comparatively well-preserved state. The myth of Enlil and Ninlil is about Enlil's serial seduction of the goddess Ninlil in various guises, resulting in the conception of the moon-god Nanna and the Underworld deities Nergal, Ninazu, and Enbilulu. Enlil was regarded as the inventor of the mattock and the patron of agriculture. Enlil also features prominently in several myths involving his son Ninurta, including Anzû and the Tablet of Destinies and Lugale.

Etymology
Enlil's name comes from ancient Sumerian EN (𒂗), meaning "lord" and LÍL (𒆤), the meaning of which is contentious, and which has sometimes been interpreted as meaning winds as a weather phenomenon (making Enlil a weather and sky god, "Lord Wind" or "Lord Storm"), or alternatively as signifying a spirit or phantom whose presence may be felt as stirring of the air, or possibly as representing a partial Semitic loanword rather than a Sumerian word at all. Enlil's name is not a genitive construction, suggesting that Enlil was seen as the personification of LÍL rather than merely the cause of LÍL.
Piotr Steinkeller has written that the meaning of LÍL may not actually be a clue to a specific divine domain of Enlil's, whether storms, spirits, or otherwise, since Enlil may have been "a typical universal god [...] without any specific domain."
Piotr Steinkeller and Piotr Michalowski have doubts about the Sumerian origin of Enlil. They have questioned the true meaning of the name, and identified Enlil with the Eblaite word I-li-lu. As noted by Manfred Krebernik and M. P. Streck; Enlil being referred to as Kur-gal (the Great Mountain) in Sumerian texts suggests he might have originated in eastern Mesopotamia.


Worship

Enlil was the patron god of the Sumerian city-state of Nippur and his main center of worship was the Ekur temple located there. The name of the temple literally means "Mountain House" in ancient Sumerian. The Ekur was believed to have been built and established by Enlil himself. It was believed to be the "mooring-rope" of heaven and earth, meaning that it was seen as "a channel of communication between earth and heaven". A hymn written during the reign of Ur-Nammu, the founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, describes the E-kur in great detail, stating that its gates were carved with scenes of Imdugud, a lesser deity sometimes shown as a giant bird, slaying a lion and an eagle snatching up a sinner.
The Sumerians believed that humanity's sole purpose was to serve the gods. They thought that a god's statue was a physical embodiment of the god
grok_lead: Enlil (ð­ðð¤), later known as Ellil in Akkadian, was a central figure in the Mesopotamian pantheon as the god of wind, air, earth, and storms, revered as the supreme king of the gods whose decrees determined the destinies of both deities and humankind. As "Lord Wind " or "Lord Air," he embodied the vital breath of life and the destructive forces of tempests, holding authority that could neither be questioned nor revoked, positioning him as the ultimate arbiter of cosmic order and kingship. Enlil's familial ties reinforced his exalted status: he was the son of the sky god An (also called Anu), the husband of the mother goddess Ninlil, and the father of major deities including the warrior god Ninurta, the moon god Nanna (Sin), and others such as Ningirsu and Ninazu, with the fire god Nusku serving as his vizier. His attributes encompassed titles like "Great Mountain," "King of All Lands," and "Father of the Gods," symbolizing his role in fostering abundance through fertile winds while also unleashing cataclysmic destruction when divine will demanded it. Enlil formed part of the supreme divine triad alongside An and Enki (Ea), representing air between sky and water, which underscored his pivotal position in maintaining the balance of the universe. The primary center of Enlil's worship was the ancient city of Nippur, where his grand temple, the Ekur ("Mountain House"), served as the spiritual heart of Sumerian religion, drawing kings from across Mesopotamia to seek his approval and legitimacy for their rule. Even as political power shifted to other cities like Babylon, where Marduk rose to prominence after around 1800 BCE, Enlil retained reverence, with his cult extending to sites such as Assur, Babylon, and Dur-Kurigalzu. His importance peaked during the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900â2350 BCE) and the Ur III dynasty (2112â2004 BCE), when Nippur functioned as the religious capital, and archaeological excavations have uncovered extensive temple complexes and inscriptions affirming his enduring influence. Enlil features prominently in Mesopotamian mythology, often as the authoritative figure driving major events. In the myth of Anzu, the monstrous bird steals the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil, disrupting cosmic order, prompting him to empower his son Ninurta to reclaim it and restore stability. In the Atrahasis epic, Enlil, disturbed by humanity's excessive noise, convenes the divine assembly to impose plagues and ultimately unleashes a great flood to curtail population growth, though Enki intervenes to save a survivor. Similarly, in the Epic of Gilgamesh, Enlil orders the deluge as punishment for human overpopulation, highlighting his role as enforcer of divine limits on mortal existence. Other texts, such as The Lament for Urim, portray him withdrawing his protection from cities, leading to their downfall, which reflects themes of divine judgment and the fragility of human prosperity. These narratives, preserved in cuneiform tablets from sites like Nippur, illustrate Enlil's dual nature as benevolent patron and stern ruler, shaping the theological worldview of ancient Mesopotamia.
